newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-G7 leaders to press for Chernobyl closure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-G7 leaders to press for Chernobyl closure.

text.p: Leaders of the world's richest industrial nations, the Group of Seven (G7), will say little about exchange rates at their economic summit this week, a German government source said on Wednesday.
But the leaders will press for timely closure of the Chernobyl nuclear power station in Ukraine, scene of the world's worst civilian nuclear accident in 1986.

G7 leaders and Russian President Boris Yeltsin will meet on June 20-22 in Denver, Colorado to discuss issues ranging from securing peace in Bosnia and how to bolster economic growth in Africa to United Nations reforms.

Financial markets are keen to hear whatever leaders from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Germany, Japan and Italy have to say about the world economy, trade issues and current exchange rates of major currencies.
In February G7 deputy leaders expressed concern about a sharp rise in the dollar, which stopped the U.S. currency's surge. The German government now does not expect G7 leaders to have much to add.
"I'm not sure whether there will be any statement about this at all," a German delegation source told reporters. "We probably won't have anything new."
Russia will be present at the group's informal meetings For the first time from the beginning.

But leaders from the traditional G7 will still issue a separate closing statement and will meet privately without Yeltsin for about 90 minutes to discuss a range of issues concerning economic and financial policies.
The key issues for German Chancellor Helmut Kohl at this year's summit will be environmental protection and ensuring the punctual closure of Chernobyl.
G7 leaders and Ukraine agreed last year on a $3.1 billion plan to build two new power plants and shut the power station down by 2000.
But the plan has been endangered by uncertainty over funding from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and other international institutions.

"We expect a concrete decision in Denver that will make clear that our goal remains to shut down Chernobyl by the year 2000," the German government source said, adding that there would be a new aid package.
Less than half the new funds would come from G7 countries and Ukraine, and the EBRD and the World Bank would have to increase their contributions to the project, he said.
Ukraine's top Chernobyl negotiator said earlier this month that the dispute over the project's financing could delay the planned closure date.

Ukraine's memorandum with the G7 to close Chernobyl in exchange for $3.1 billion was signed last year just before the 10th anniversary of the April 26, 1986 disaster which sent a radiation cloud over neighbouring Russia, Belarus and much of the rest of Europe.
The G7 is to consider a $780 million project to stabilise the concrete "sarcophagus" enclosing the ruined fourth reactor.
Other environmental issues the Germans will address include a restructuring of United Nations environmental programmes to give them more clout and make them more efficient.

Germany also wants the G7 plus Russia to agree on setting a target for reducing the gases that cause global warming by 15 percent by the year 2010, compared with reference levels in 1990, as the European Union agreed this week at its Amsterdam summit.
Bonn also backed a plan announced by U.S. President Bill Clinton on Tuesday that would ease trade barriers for African nations that are carrying out political and market reforms.
"Africa as a whole will show annual economic growth of four to five percent. This is a positive development," the German official said.
-- william.boston@reuters.com (Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097 150)
